Being a Grandparent Without Taking Over

For grandparents who want to help without stepping on the parents. It asks how they do it before offering how you did, spends your one opinion carefully, finds something that is yours with the child, and offers an evening rather than advice.

Grandparenting · Family · Boundaries · Relationships · 9 items · once a week

The checklist

  • Ask how they do it before offering how you did — their house, their rules, even when yours worked.
  • Say yes to the help they actually asked for — the useful kind is rarely the kind you imagined.
  • Keep the comment about the feeding to yourself — you get one opinion a month, so spend it well.
  • Have one thing that is yours with the child — a walk, a recipe, a game nobody else plays.
  • Give the parents an evening, not advice — two hours off is worth more than any suggestion.
  • Ask before the sweets and the screen time — undermining is usually accidental and still lands.
  • Let the parent correct you in front of the child — backing them up is the whole job here.
  • Say what you can and cannot manage honestly — a grandparent stretched thin helps nobody.
  • Remember you are not the one in charge now — that loss is real and worth sitting with quietly.

Use this checklist Free account: tick items off and keep each day's record.

How to use it

Run through it once a week, honestly and without scoring yourself. A checklist is a way of noticing, not a test: an item you cannot tick is information about the day, not a verdict on you. Over a few weeks the pattern of what gets ticked and what does not says more than any single pass.

With a free Theraglee account the checklist remembers each pass, so you can look back. Without one, you can still read it here and keep your own copy.
